assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices (BLP) and dynamic oligopoly estimation changed how demand, market power, mergers and welfare are measured. The methods are standard in industrial organisation, antitrust, trade and health economics, and are used by practitioners and regulators.
assessment.attribution: The core is the Berry (1994) inversion, Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes (1995), and Pakes's work on dynamic games and estimation (Ericson-Pakes, Pakes-McGuire). Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are also important contributors, so a three-person cap leaves out real contributors. The three named are the clearest core.
assessment.maturity: The central work dates from the 1990s and has had decades of validation, extension and wide adoption. Timing is not a constraint.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee would prefer to credit Bresnahan or the entry-model contributions (Bresnahan-Reiss) over Levinsohn.
Identification and instrument-validity critiques of BLP-type models, though these are largely methodological refinements.
I cannot independently verify citation or adoption figures from the supplied evidence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work established modern political economics: it analyses how electoral rules, constitutions and political institutions shape fiscal policy, public goods provision and state capacity. It combines formal theory with empirical tests and has influenced comparative politics, public finance and development.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central joint authors of the field-defining synthesis (The Economic Effects of Constitutions, Political Economics). Besley's work on accountability, state capacity and development is closely related and independently important. The grouping is coherent and fits within three.
assessment.maturity: The work spans the mid-1990s to the 2010s. It is well established, with a long record of replication and extension.
uncertainties: Some constitutional-effects findings rest on cross-country identification that has been contested.
Credit could be split differently between this group and other political-economy contributors not listed.
Committee appetite for political economics after the 2024 prize on institutions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities underlies modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. Staggered contracts, Calvo pricing, the interest-rate rule and the micro-founded policy framework have had very large practical and academic influence.
assessment.attribution: Credit is diffuse. Calvo (1983) and Taylor (1980) supply the time-dependent pricing models. Taylor also supplied the policy rule and Woodford the micro-founded synthesis. Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans, Gali, Gertler and Smets-Wouters are important quantitative and empirical contributors. Selecting three necessarily omits contributors with large claims.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1980s to the 2000s and is thoroughly validated in practice, so maturity is not an issue. Because it has already been extensively recognised in the field, the main question is attribution.
uncertainties: Attribution among many comparable contributors is difficult and may lower the odds of a clean three-person prize.
Debates over the post-2021 inflation episode and the empirical fit of the Phillips curve.
Previous prizes to related macroeconomists may reduce room for this area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade theory showed that exporting is concentrated in a few productive firms, and that trade liberalisation reallocates activity toward them. This reshaped the theory, measurement and policy analysis of gains from trade and connects naturally to micro data.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) and Helpman's broader work on trade with differentiated products and firm-level behaviour complement it. Redding is credited here but I would include him only if a third laureate is needed. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have related empirical priority claims that are not on this ballot entry.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from about 2003 and has more than two decades of empirical validation and extension, which is sufficient for recognition.
uncertainties: Priority and overlap with the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum empirical work, which is not credited here.
Helpman also appears in another entry (B044), which affects how the field would be split.
Krugman's earlier prize may make the Committee view this as a continuation of the same line.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work turned optimal tax theory into an empirically implementable framework. It uses the sufficient-statistics approach, taxable-income elasticities and evidence on behavioural responses, and it has influenced tax policy debates and empirical public finance.
assessment.attribution: Saez's work on optimal income taxation and taxable-income responses, together with Chetty's sufficient-statistics formulation, forms the core. Slemrod and Feldstein-style elasticity work have strong earlier claims, and Stantcheva is a more recent contributor. Both Saez and Chetty also appear in other entries (B020, B010), which complicates comparison across the list.
assessment.maturity: The work is largely from the 2000s to the 2010s. Empirical validation and policy uptake are substantial, but the sufficient-statistics programme is still developing.
uncertainties: Whether elasticity estimates are robust enough for the policy conclusions drawn.
Overlap in credited people with other entries could lead the Committee to prefer a different bundling.
Slemrod and earlier optimal-tax theorists could be seen as having stronger priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Task-based accounts of technology and the measurement of local labour-market effects of import competition changed understanding of wage inequality, polarisation and the distributional costs of trade. The work has had broad influence on policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor's contributions on skill demand and tasks (with Levy and Murnane) and Autor-Dorn-Hanson on the China shock are the core. Katz's earlier work on skill-biased technological change and wage structure is also significant. Acemoglu's related task framework was recognised in a previous prize, which affects credit allocation. Dorn is a key coauthor.
assessment.maturity: The work is mainly from 2003 to the 2010s. It is well established, but long-run effects and some interpretations are still being debated.
uncertainties: Debate over the size and persistence of China-shock effects and the empirical identification strategy.
Overlap with the 2024 recognition of institutions and growth and the 2021 labour-economics prize may affect Committee appetite.
Choosing between Autor, Hanson, Dorn and Katz is hard.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law-and-finance programme documented how investor protection and legal origins relate to financial development, ownership structure and growth. It opened a large literature on institutions and corporate governance. Its explanatory claims are partly contested.
assessment.attribution: La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny (LLSV) wrote the foundational papers jointly, so a cap of three omits Vishny, whose claim is equal on the papers. The group is coherent but credit is not easily separable. Shleifer also has independent contributions in behavioural finance.
assessment.maturity: The foundational work is from 1997 to 2008. It has been thoroughly debated, with replication and critique of the legal-origins measures and causal interpretation.
uncertainties: Serious critiques of the coding of legal rules and of the causal claim that legal origin drives outcomes.
Cap of three laureates versus four jointly credited authors.
Reputational and ethics controversies surrounding some of the authors that the Committee might consider.
My field proximity (corporate finance) could bias me, so I treat this cautiously.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence on reciprocity, fairness and inequity aversion, with formal models such as Fehr-Schmidt, showed systematic departures from purely selfish behaviour and helped explain contracts, cooperation and punishment. Experimental design and theory were integrated and the work has influenced several subfields.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is the central empirical and conceptual figure. Fehr-Schmidt (1999) provides the best-known model, and Falk is a major collaborator, particularly on field evidence. Rabin (1993) and Bolton-Ockenfels (2000) have parallel claims not on this entry, as do the earlier Güth ultimatum-game experiments.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the late 1990s to the 2010s. It is well replicated in the laboratory, with ongoing debate about field external validity.
uncertainties: External validity of laboratory social-preference results and the stability of parameter estimates.
Priority claims of Rabin and Bolton-Ockenfels, and possible overlap with earlier behavioural prizes.
Whether the Committee would credit theory or experiments, which would change the laureate set.
